questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] (x^2 + 3x) = lim[x->2] x^2 + lim[x->2] 3x$
questions.explain: Sum law.

questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] 3x = 3 lim[x->2] x$
questions.explain: Constant multiple law.

questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] x^2 = (lim[x->2] x)^2$
questions.explain: Power law.

questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] frac{x}{x + 1} = frac{lim[x->2] x}{lim[x->2] (x + 1)}$
questions.explain: Quotient law.

questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] x(x + 1) = (lim[x->2] x)(lim[x->2] (x + 1))$
questions.explain: Product law.

questions.text: Which law justifies this step? $lim[x->2] sqrt(x + 7) = sqrt(lim[x->2] (x + 7))$
questions.explain: Root law.

slides.text: If $lim[x->a] f(x)$ and $lim[x->a] g(x)$ both **exist**, limits split apart. Match each limit to what it equals.
slides.hint: Limits pass right through sums, constants, products and quotients.
slides.explain: Plus: powers and roots pass through too.
